## Three outbreaks, the same problems

- **COVID-19, 2020.** $R_t$, the number of new infections per infected
  person, daily for thousands of locations. Weekly to SPI-M-O, the
  UK government's modelling advisers
- **mpox, 2022.** Nowcasting for UKHSA. Nowcasting is estimating what
  has already happened but has not yet been reported
- **Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of
  the Congo (DRC), 2026.** One joint model across five data streams,
  refit on every push
- Each time the methods from the last outbreak were not reusable
- Each time the models did not fit the data sources that existed, and
  the data changed under us

![](../figures/exchange-timeline.png){width="72%" fig-align="center"
fig-alt="A timeline from 1760 to 2026 in two panels with an axis break.
Grey dots for Bernoulli 1760, Ross 1911, Kermack and McKendrick 1927,
Anderson and May 1991, foot and mouth 2001, H1N1 2009 and Ebola in West
Africa 2014. Teal dots, marked work I was part of, for COVID-19 in 2020,
mpox in 2022 and Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in 2026."}

::: {.attribution}
Abbott et al. 2020, Wellcome Open Research · Overton et al. 2023, PLoS
Comput Biol · [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd] · dates in
`notes/research-history.md`, drawn by `scripts/keynote-timeline.py`
:::

## What I work on

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Composable models.** Components that can be reused across contexts
  and combined into joint models, with the uncertainty carried through
- **Improving outbreak modelling.** Methods that survive from one
  outbreak to the next. Models that fit the data sources that exist
- **A workflow for modelling with multiple data sources.** Data sources
  added one at a time, with the checks and feedback loops written down
- Joint models give better evidence than chains of separate models.
  Building one during an outbreak is slow and needs several kinds of
  expertise
- In R and Stan first. In Julia now
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-workflow-lego.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Four columns of building blocks. Process models: three renewal
variants. Observation models: eight ways to link infections to counts,
with delays and ascertainment. Inference and computation choices, from
HMC to synthetic likelihood. Data integration choices, from ensembling
to full joint modelling. The four snap together at the bottom right."}

::: {.attribution}
Figure 6 of Abbott et al., [A workflow for infectious disease
modelling][wf] · [epiaware.org](https://epiaware.org) · Lison et al.
2024, PLoS Comput Biol
:::
:::
::::

## Where the tools get used

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Consulting.** Time with CDC collaborators, UKHSA, and state and
  local public health departments in the US
- The aim is to add other countries' public health departments
- **In outbreaks.** `epidist` in the DRC response's correspondence in
  the New England Journal of Medicine this August
- Several teams used the tools in Exercise Pegasus, the UK's 2025
  national pandemic exercise
- **Next.** Tools flexible and extensible enough to be easy for a large
  language model to use
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-public-health-use.png){width="100%"

## epiforecasts and the epinowcast community

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- **epiforecasts.** Led by Sebastian Funk at LSHTM. Real-time modelling
  and evaluating it
- `EpiNow2`, `scoringutils`, and the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub
  from 2021, now RespiCast at the European Centre for Disease
  Prevention and Control (ECDC)
- 2020 to 2022, weekly $R_t$ estimates and forecasts to SPI-M-O
- **epinowcast.** A forum of over 50 researchers and public health
  analysts
- A monthly seminar since May 2023, 31 so far, organised with Clara
  Brigitta and Fanny Bergström
- In 2023 I wrote: "community >> methods or models alone"
